crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms
children.blurb: An AI enablement audit in an investment firm maps where artificial intelligence and machine learning are used across the investment lifecycle, from research and portfolio construction to trading, operations, compliance and client reporting.

children.name: Fair Lending and Bias Testing
children.blurb: Fair lending and bias testing covers how lenders and credit decision systems evaluate applicants without unlawful disparate treatment or disparate impact on protected characteristics such as race, national origin, sex, marital status, age, or receipt of public assistance.

children.name: Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients
children.blurb: Explaining models to regulators and clients covers the practice of translating how a model works, what data it uses, and what its outputs mean into language that a non-specialist can act on.

children.name: Protecting Material Non-Public Information
children.blurb: Protecting material non-public information in AI-related firms covers the handling of confidential data about models, training runs, partnerships, regulatory findings, and financial results before public disclosure.

children.name: Verifying What a Model Produced
children.blurb: Verifying what a model produced covers the practices used to confirm that an AI system's outputs are accurate, consistent with their inputs, and fit for the purpose a firm assigns them.

sections.body: Governance and fiduciary risk covers the controls an investment firm puts around artificial intelligence before and after it is used. In practice, this means running an enablement audit that checks data sources, model permissions, and access rights before a tool is approved. Fair lending testing applies statistical tests to model outputs to see whether approval rates or pricing differ by protected class. Explaining models to regulators and clients means producing plain language descriptions of what inputs matter and how outputs are reached. Data loss prevention scans prompts and model responses for material non-public information, and verification logs the model version, inputs, and outputs so a firm can show what was produced.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is partly standardized and partly still open. Audit checklists and bias testing metrics such as adverse impact ratios are widely used, and model documentation is now common. What is not solved is that explanations are approximations of a model's behavior, not a full account of its internal logic. Bias tests can miss proxy variables or combinations of characteristics that produce unfair results. Data loss prevention can catch known patterns like account numbers, but it is weaker against paraphrased or indirect leaks. The 214 compliance and regulation pages tracked on this site reflect how fragmented and changing the rules remain, so no single review can guarantee a model stays compliant.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader would start with The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms, which describes the pre-deployment review that sets the baseline for the other controls. Fair Lending and Bias Testing goes deeper into the statistical checks used for credit and pricing models, and it is the page to consult when a model makes decisions about consumers. Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients covers the documentation and plain language summaries that satisfy oversight requests. Protecting Material Non-Public Information addresses the data loss prevention and access controls that keep confidential data out of prompts and outputs. Verifying What a Model Produced closes the loop by explaining how logs and audit trails prove what a model actually did, which supports the enablement audit and any later dispute.
